title: Geometry and Curves
summary: Vector calculus starts with the geometry of space. In this chapter we build the tools that all later chapters use: dot and cross products, lines and planes, surfaces, and curves with their curvature. Every formula here has a picture; keep the pictures in mind.

intro.x: Vector calculus starts with the geometry of space. In this chapter we build the tools that all later chapters use: dot and cross products, lines and planes, surfaces, and curves with their curvature. Every formula here has a picture; keep the pictures in mind.

The dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way. It is positive when the angle is acute, zero when the vectors are perpendicular, and negative when the angle is obtuse. If $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are linearly independent, then
\det\bigl[\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b\bigr]=\norm{\vec a\times\vec b}^2>0 ,
where the determinant has the three vectors as rows. So $(\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b)$ is a right-handed triple, like $(\ihat,\jhat,\khat)$.

Expand the determinant along the third row $\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b$ with entries $c_1,c_2,c_3$. The cofactors of the entries in the third row are exactly the components $c_1,c_2,c_3$ of $\vec a\times\vec b$ (compare with the definition). Therefore the determinant equals $c_1^2+c_2^2+c_3^2=\norm{\vec a\times\vec b}^2$, which is positive because $\vec a\times\vec b\neq\vec 0$ by Theorem 1.8(c).

blocks.x: The cross product exists only in $\R^3$ (in the form used here). It is not associative: $\ihat\times(\ihat\times\jhat)=\ihat\times\khat=-\jhat$, but $(\ihat\times\ihat)\times\jhat=\vec 0$. Also, $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec a\times\vec c$ does not imply $\vec b=\vec c$ (take $\vec c=\vec b+\vec a$).
$[\vec a,\vec b,\vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Triple product as determinant and volume

blocks.x: \vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=\det\begin{pmatrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\\c_1&c_2&c_3\end{pmatrix}.

Consequently the scalar triple product is unchanged by a cyclic permutation, $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b\cdot(\vec c\times\vec a)=\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)$, and the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ is $\abs{\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)}$.
Expand the determinant along its first row:
a_1(b_2c_3-b_3c_2)-a_2(b_1c_3-b_3c_1)+a_3(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)=a_1(\vec b\times\vec c)_1+a_2(\vec b\times\vec c)_2+a_3(\vec b\times\vec c)_3,
which is $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$. A cyclic permutation of rows is an even permutation, so it does not change the determinant; this proves the cyclic property.

For the volume, take $\vec b,\vec c$ as the base. The base area is $\norm{\vec b\times\vec c}$ by Theorem 1.8(c). The vector $\vec b\times\vec c$ is perpendicular to the base, so the height of the parallelepiped is the length of the projection of $\vec a$ on the direction $\hat{\vec n}=(\vec b\times\vec c)/\norm{\vec b\times\vec c}$, that is $h=\abs{\vec a\cdot\hat{\vec n}}$. Therefore
\Vol=\text{base}\times\text{height}=\norm{\vec b\times\vec c}\,\abs{\vec a\cdot\hat{\vec n}}=\abs{\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)}.

blocks.caption: The parallelepiped spanned by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$. The base is the parallelogram of $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ with area $\norm{\vec b\times\vec c}$; the height $h$ is the component of $\vec a$ along $\vec b\times\vec c$. So the volume is $\abs{\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)}$.

A line through the point $\vec r_0$ with direction $\vec d\ne\vec 0$ is the set
\vec r(t)=\vec r_0+t\,\vec d,\qquad t\in\R .
A plane through $\vec r_0$ with normal vector $\vec n\neq\vec0$ is the set of points $\vec r$ with
\vec n\cdot(\vec r-\vec r_0)=0,\quad\text{that is}\quad n_1x+n_2y+n_3z=d\ \ (d=\vec n\cdot\vec r_0).

The plane is the set of all points $\vec r$ such that the vector $\vec r-\vec r_0$ is perpendicular to $\vec n$. If the plane is given by two direction vectors $\vec u,\vec v$ (not parallel), then $\vec n=\vec u\times\vec v$ is a normal vector.
Let $P$ be a point with position vector $\vec p$.
The distance from $P$ to the plane $\vec n\cdot(\vec r-\vec r_0)=0$ is $\displaystyle\frac{\abs{\vec n\cdot(\vec p-\vec r_0)}}{\norm{\vec n}}$.
The distance from $P$ to the line $\vec r_0+t\vec d$ is $\displaystyle\frac{\norm{\vec d\times(\vec p-\vec r_0)}}{\norm{\vec d}}$.

(a) Let $\vec w=\vec p-\vec r_0$ and let $\vec m=\vec n/\norm{\vec n}$ be the unit normal. Take any point $\vec q$ of the plane, so $\vec n\cdot(\vec q-\vec r_0)=0$. Then $\vec p-\vec q=\vec w-(\vec q-\vec r_0)$, and its component along $\vec m$ is
(\vec p-\vec q)\cdot\vec m=\vec w\cdot\vec m-(\vec q-\vec r_0)\cdot\vec m=\vec w\cdot\vec m .

For a unit vector $\vec m$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $
orm{\vec p-\vec q}\ge\abs{(\vec p-\vec q)\cdot\vec m}=\abs{\vec w\cdot\vec m}$. So every point of the plane is at least $\abs{\vec w\cdot\vec m}$ away from $P$. This bound is reached: the point $\vec q_0=\vec p-(\vec w\cdot\vec m)\vec m$ lies in the plane, because $\vec n\cdot(\vec q_0-\vec r_0)=\vec n\cdot\vec w-(\vec w\cdot\vec m)\,\vec n\cdot\vec m=\vec n\cdot\vec w-(\vec w\cdot\vec n)=0$, and $
orm{\vec p-\vec q_0}=\abs{\vec w\cdot\vec m}$. Hence the distance is $\abs{\vec w\cdot\vec m}=\abs{\vec n\cdot\vec w}/
orm{\vec n}$.

orm{\vec d	imes\vec w}$ (Theorem 1.8(c)). Taking $\vec d$ as the base, the area also equals $
orm{\vec d}\cdot h$, where $h$ is the height, that is the distance from $P$ to the line through the base. Hence $h=
orm{\vec d	imes\vec w}/

blocks.x: A surface in $\R^3$ can be described in two main ways.
Implicitly, as a level set $\{(x,y,z):F(x,y,z)=c\}$. Example: the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2$.

Parametrically, as the image of a map $\vec r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v))$ from a region of the $(u,v)$-plane. Example: the same sphere is $\vec r(\theta,\varphi)=R(\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\ \sin\varphi\sin\theta,\ \cos\varphi)$, with $0\le\theta<2\pi$, $0\le\varphi\le\pi$.

blocks.caption: The unit sphere. It is the level set $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$, and also the image of the parametrization $(\theta,\varphi)\mapsto(\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\cos\varphi)$. Blue curves have constant $\varphi$ (latitudes); orange curves have constant $\theta$ (longitudes).

blocks.x: The two descriptions answer different questions. An implicit equation makes it easy to test whether a point is on the surface (plug it in). A parametric form makes it easy to generate points and to integrate over the surface (we do this in Chapter 6).

A parametric curve is a map $\vec r:[a,b] o\R^3$, $\vec r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t))$. It is $C^1$ if $x,y,z$ have continuous derivatives. The vector $\vec r\,'(t)=(x',y',z')$ is the velocity, and $ orm{\vec r\,'(t)}$ is the speed. The curve is regular (or smooth) if $\vec r\,'(t) eq\vec 0$ for all $t$. For a regular curve, the unit tangent vector is $\vec T(t)=\vec r\,'(t)/ orm{\vec r\,'(t)}$.

The circle of radius $R$: $\vec r(t)=(R\cos t,R\sin t)$, with $\vec r\,'(t)=(-R\sin t,R\cos t)$ and constant speed $R$. The helix $\vec r(t)=(a\cos t,a\sin t,bt)$ has $\vec r\,'(t)=(-a\sin t,a\cos t,b)$ and constant speed $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

blocks.caption: A helix $\vec r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0.15t)$. The tangent vector $\vec T$ is always inclined at the same angle to the horizontal; the curve winds around the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$.

blocks.x: Arc length
How long is a curve? We define length by approximating the curve with a polygon.
Let $P=\{a=t_0length of the inscribed polygon is $L(P)=\sum_{i=1}^n\norm{\vec r(t_i)-\vec r(t_{i-1})}$. The arc length of the curve is $L=\sup_P L(P)$.
For a $C^1$ curve $\vec r:[a,b]\to\R^3$,
L=\int_a^b\norm{\vec r\,'(t)}\,\dd t .

Step 1: $L(P)\le\int_a^b orm{\vec r\,'}$ for every partition. By the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to each component, $\vec r(t_i)-\vec r(t_{i-1})=\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\vec r\,'(s)\,\dd s$. For a vector-valued integral, $ orm{\int\vec f}\le\int orm{\vec f}$. (Proof: let $\vec v=\int\vec f$; then $ orm{\vec v}^2=\vec v\cdot\int\vec f=\int\vec v\cdot\vec f\le\int orm{\vec v} orm{\vec f}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz; divide by $ orm{\vec v}$ if $\vec v e\vec 0$.) So $ orm{\vec r(t_i)-\vec r(t_{i-1})}\le\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} orm{\vec r\,'}$. Summing over $i$ gives the claim. Taking the supremum, $L\le\int_a^b orm{\vec r\,'}$.

Step 2: the reverse inequality. Let $\eps>0$. The function $\vec r\,'$ is continuous on the compact interval $[a,b]$, hence uniformly continuous: there is $\delta>0$ such that $\norm{\vec r\,'(s)-\vec r\,'(t)}<\eps$ whenever $\abs{s-t}<\delta$. Take a partition with mesh smaller than $\delta$. For each $i$,
\vec r(t_i)-\vec r(t_{i-1})=\vec r\,'(t_i)\,\Delta t_i+\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\bigl(\vec r\,'(s)-\vec r\,'(t_i)\bigr)\dd s,
and the last integral has norm at most $\eps\,\Delta t_i$. By the triangle inequality
\norm{\vec r(t_i)-\vec r(t_{i-1})}\ge\norm{\vec r\,'(t_i)}\Delta t_i-\eps\,\Delta t_i .

Summing, $L\ge L(P)\ge\sum_i
orm{\vec r\,'(t_i)}\Delta t_i-\eps(b-a)$. The sum is a Riemann sum of the continuous function $
orm{\vec r\,'}$; as the mesh goes to $0$ it tends to $\int_a^b
orm{\vec r\,'}$. Hence $L\ge\int_a^b
orm{\vec r\,'}-\eps(b-a)$ for every $\eps>0$, so $L\ge\int_a^b
orm{\vec r\,'}$.

For a regular curve, define the arc-length function $s(t)=\int_a^t orm{\vec r\,'(u)}\dd u$. Since $s'(t)= orm{\vec r\,'(t)}>0$, the function $s$ is strictly increasing and can be inverted. Using $s$ as the parameter, the curve has unit speed: $ orm{\dd\vec r/\dd s}=1$. This is the arc-length parametrization. It is the natural choice for studying shape, because it does not depend on how fast we travel.

sections.title: Curvature, normal and binormal; the Frenet–Serret equations

blocks.x: From now on, let $\vec r(s)$ be a curve parametrized by arc length, and write a prime for $\dd/\dd s$. Then $\vec T=\vec r\,'$ is the unit tangent.
If $\vec u(s)$ is a differentiable vector with constant length, then $\vec u\cdot\vec u\,'=0$.
Differentiate $\vec u\cdot\vec u=\text{const}$: $2\,\vec u\cdot\vec u\,'=0$.
Since $\norm{\vec T}=1$, the lemma gives $\vec T\cdot\vec T\,'=0$: the derivative of $\vec T$ is perpendicular to $\vec T$. It measures how fast the direction of the curve changes.

The curvature is $\kappa(s)=\norm{\vec T\,'(s)}$. Where $\kappa\ne0$, the principal normal is $\vec N=\vec T\,'/\kappa$, and the binormal is $\vec B=\vec T\times\vec N$. The radius of curvature is $1/\kappa$.

The three vectors $\vec T,\vec N,\vec B$ are mutually perpendicular unit vectors, and $(\vec T,\vec N,\vec B)$ is right-handed (Proposition 1.9). They form the Frenet frame: a moving coordinate system that travels along the curve. The plane spanned by $\vec T$ and $\vec N$ is the osculating plane.

blocks.caption: The osculating circle (dashed) touches the curve at $P$ and has the same tangent and the same curvature there. Its radius is $R=1/\kappa$, and its centre lies on the normal $\vec N$. The curve here is $y=x^2/2$ at $x=0.5$.

blocks.x: Let $\vec r(s)$ be a regular unit-speed curve with $\kappa>0$ and assume $\vec N$ is differentiable. There is a function $\tau(s)$, called the torsion, such that

The first equation is the definition of $\vec N$. The vectors $\vec T,\vec N,\vec B$ are orthonormal, so every vector can be written as a combination of them, and the coefficient of a vector $\vec w$ along $\vec e\in\{\vec T,\vec N,\vec B\}$ is $\vec w\cdot\vec e$. Differentiate the relations $\vec e_i\cdot\vec e_j=\delta_{ij}$ to get
\vec e_i\,'\cdot\vec e_j+\vec e_i\cdot\vec e_j\,'=0 .

So the matrix of coefficients $A_{ij}=\vec e_i\,'\cdot\vec e_j$ is antisymmetric: $A_{ij}=-A_{ji}$ and $A_{ii}=0$. We know $A_{TN}=\vec T\,'\cdot\vec N=\kappa$ and $A_{TB}=\vec T\,'\cdot\vec B=\kappa\,\vec N\cdot\vec B=0$. By antisymmetry, $A_{NT}=-\kappa$ and $A_{BT}=0$. Define $\tau=A_{NB}=\vec N\,'\cdot\vec B$. Then $A_{BN}=-\tau$. Therefore

Curvature $\kappa$ measures how fast the curve bends inside its osculating plane. Torsion $\tau$ measures how fast the curve twists out of that plane. A curve is planar if and only if $\tau\equiv0$. A straight line has $\kappa=0$. A circle has $\kappa=1/R$ and $\tau=0$. A helix has constant $\kappa$ and constant $\tau$.
Most curves are not given with arc length as a parameter. The next theorem gives $\kappa$ and $\tau$ for any regular parametrization.

Frenet–Serret: $\vec T'=\kappa\vec N$, $\vec N'=-\kappa\vec T+\tau\vec B$, $\vec B'=-\tau\vec N$. General formulas: $\kappa=\norm{\vec r'\times\vec r''}/\norm{\vec r'}^3$.
What does the cross product mean geometrically? A vector perpendicular to both factors; length = area of the parallelogram; direction by the right-hand rule.
Why does $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$ give a volume? Base area $\norm{\vec b\times\vec c}$ times the height (component of $\vec a$ along the normal).
How do you find the distance from a point to a plane? Project the vector from a plane point onto the unit normal.
What is curvature? The rate of turning of the unit tangent per unit arc length; the inverse of the radius of the osculating circle.
Why is $\vec T'$ perpendicular to $\vec T$? Because $\vec T$ has constant length (differentiate $\vec T\cdot\vec T=1$).
What does torsion measure? How fast the curve leaves its osculating plane; $\tau=0$ for planar curves.
Exercises
Prove the parallelogram law: $ orm{\vec a+\vec b}^2+ orm{\vec a-\vec b}^2=2 orm{\vec a}^2+2 orm{\vec b}^2$.
Prove the Jacobi identity $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)+\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a)+\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec 0$. (Hint: use Theorem 1.12 three times.)

Find the distance between two skew lines $\vec r_1+t\vec d_1$ and $\vec r_2+s\vec d_2$. (Answer: $\abs{(\vec r_2-\vec r_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)}/\norm{\vec d_1\times\vec d_2}$. Explain why using Theorem 1.11.)
Compute the arc length of $\vec r(t)=(t,\ t^2/2)$ for $0\le t\le 1$ and find its curvature at $t=1$.
Show that a regular curve with $\tau\equiv0$ and $\kappa>0$ lies in a plane. (Hint: Frenet–Serret gives $\vec B'=\vec 0$; consider $\vec r\cdot\vec B$.)
